[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#191)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#194)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

Additionally the returned object can be safely mutated, the changes are guaranteed to be reflected in the input array.

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

# FinalizationRegistry in js_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/js-sys/0.3.103/js_sys/struct.FinalizationRegistry.html

`pub struct FinalizationRegistry { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The `FinalizationRegistry` object lets you request a callback when an
object is garbage-collected.

`FinalizationRegistry` provides a way to request that a cleanup
callback get called at some point when an object registered with the
registry has been reclaimed (garbage-collected). Cleanup callbacks
are sometimes called *finalizers*.

Avoid where possible: cleanup callbacks should not be relied upon for anything essential. They are best used to reduce memory usage over the course of a program for objects that benefit from cleanup. Whether, when, and in what order callbacks fire is implementation-defined.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Creates a new `FinalizationRegistry` with the given cleanup callback.

The cleanup callback is invoked, at some point after a registered
target is garbage-collected, with the `held_value` that was passed to
[ FinalizationRegistry::register](https://docs.rs/struct.FinalizationRegistry.html#method.register). Because callbacks may be deferred
or skipped entirely, the callback should normally outlive the

`FinalizationRegistry` (for example by being created via
[).](https://docs.rs/struct.Function.html#method.from_closure)

`Function::from_closure`[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#4950)#### pub fn [register_with_token](https://docs.rs#method.register_with_token)(

    unregister_token: &[JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html),

`unregister_token` that can later be passed to

`target` and `unregister_token` must be objects (or non-registered
symbols), and the same value may be passed for both.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

Creates an array from raw IEEE 754 binary16 bit patterns.

This pairs naturally with the optional `half` crate:

```
use half::f16;
use js_sys::Float16Array;
let values = [f16::from_f32(1.0), f16::from_f32(-2.0)];
let bits = values.map(f16::to_bits);
let array = Float16Array::new_from_u16_slice(&bits);
```

Creates a JS typed array which is a view into wasm’s linear memory at the slice specified.

This function returns a new typed array which is a view into wasm’s memory. This view does not copy the underlying data.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Views into WebAssembly memory are only valid so long as the
backing buffer isn’t resized in JS. Once this function is called
any future calls to `Box::new` (or malloc of any form) may cause
the returned value here to be invalidated. Use with caution!

Additionally the returned object can be safely mutated but the input slice isn’t guaranteed to be mutable.

Finally, the returned object is disconnected from the input slice’s lifetime, so there’s no guarantee that the data is read at the right time.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#14136-14180)#### pub unsafe fn [view_mut_raw](https://docs.rs#method.view_mut_raw)(ptr: [*mut ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html)[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html), length: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [Float32Array](https://docs.rs/struct.Float32Array.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#188)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#191)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#194)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

Creates a JS typed array which is a view into wasm’s linear memory at the slice specified.

This function returns a new typed array which is a view into wasm’s memory. This view does not copy the underlying data.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Views into WebAssembly memory are only valid so long as the
backing buffer isn’t resized in JS. Once this function is called
any future calls to `Box::new` (or malloc of any form) may cause
the returned value here to be invalidated. Use with caution!

Additionally the returned object can be safely mutated but the input slice isn’t guaranteed to be mutable.

Finally, the returned object is disconnected from the input slice’s lifetime, so there’s no guarantee that the data is read at the right time.

Views into WebAssembly memory are only valid so long as the

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#188)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#191)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#194)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

# Function in js_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/js-sys/0.3.103/js_sys/struct.Function.html

`pub struct Function<T: `[JsFunction](https://docs.rs/trait.JsFunction.html) = [fn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.fn.html)([JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html), [JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html), [JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html), [JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html), [JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html), [JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html), [JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html), [JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html)) -> [JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html)> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

`Function` represents any generic Function in JS, by treating all arguments as `JsValue`.

It takes a generic parameter of phantom type `fn (Arg1, ..., Argn) -> Ret` which
is used to type the JS function. For example, `Function<fn () -> Number>` represents
a function taking no arguments that returns a number.

The 8 generic argument parameters (`Arg1` through `Arg8`) are the argument
types. Arguments not provided enable strict arity checking at compile time.

A void function is represented by `fn (Arg) -> Undefined`, and **not** the `()` unit
type. This is because generics must be based on JS values in the JS generic type system.

*The default without any parameters is as a void function - no arguments,  Undefined return.*

*The default generic for  Function is fn (JsValue, JsValue, ...) -> JsValue,
representing any function, since all functions safely upcast into this function.*

[§](https://docs.rs#arity-enforcement)Arity Enforcement

It is not possible to use `call4` or `bind4` on a function that does not have
at least 4 arguments — the compiler will reject this because only arguments that
are not `None` support the trait bound for `ErasableGeneric`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// A function taking no args, returning Number
let f: Function<Number> = get_some_fn();
// A function taking (String, Number) and returning Boolean
let f: Function<Boolean, String, Number> = get_some_fn();
## Upcasting
To pass a typed `Function` where a different generic Function is expected, `upcast()` may be used
to convert into any generic `Function` at zero cost with type-safety.
MDN documentation (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Function)
```

constructor directly can create functions dynamically, but suffers from
security and similar (but far less significant) performance issues
similar to `eval`. However, unlike `eval`, the `Function` constructor
allows executing code in the global scope, prompting better programming
habits and allowing for more efficient code minification.

### impl<T: [JsFunction](https://docs.rs/trait.JsFunction.html)> [Function](https://docs.rs/struct.Function.html)<T>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#4802-4804)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#4802-4804)

The `call()` method calls a function with a given `this` value and
arguments provided as a tuple.

This method accepts a tuple of references matching the function’s argument types.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// 0-arg function
let f: Function<fn() -> Number> = get_fn();
let result = f.call(&JsValue::NULL, ())?;
// 1-arg function (note trailing comma for 1-tuple)
let f: Function<fn(JsString) -> Number> = get_fn();
let result = f.call(&JsValue::NULL, (&name,))?;
// 2-arg function
let f: Function<fn(JsString, Boolean) -> Number> = get_fn();
let result = f.call(&JsValue::NULL, (&name, &flag))?;
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#4829-4831)#### pub fn [bindn](https://docs.rs#method.bindn)<Args: [JsArgs](https://docs.rs/trait.JsArgs.html)<T>>(
    &self,

    args: Args,
) -> Args::[BindOutput](https://docs.rs/trait.JsArgs.html#associatedtype.BindOutput)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#4829-4831)

#### pub fn [bindn](https://docs.rs#method.bindn)<Args: [JsArgs](https://docs.rs/trait.JsArgs.html)<T>>(
    &self,
    context: &[JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html),
    args: Args,
) -> Args::[BindOutput](https://docs.rs/trait.JsArgs.html#associatedtype.BindOutput)

The `bind()` method creates a new function that, when called, has its
`this` keyword set to the provided value, with a given sequence of
arguments preceding any provided when the new function is called.

This method accepts a tuple of references to bind.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let f: Function<fn(JsString, Boolean) -> Number> = get_fn();
// Bind no args - same signature
let bound: Function<fn(JsString, Boolean) -> Number> = f.bind(&ctx, ());
// Bind one arg (use 1-tuple of references)
let bound: Function<fn(Boolean) -> Number> = f.bind(&ctx, (&my_string,));
// Bind two args - becomes 0-arg function
let bound: Function<fn() -> Number> = f.bind(&ctx, (&my_string, &my_bool));
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#4895-4902)#### pub fn [closure_ref](https://docs.rs#method.closure_ref)<'a, C>(closure: &'a [ScopedClosure](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/closure/struct.ScopedClosure.html)<'_, C>) -> &'a Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#4895-4902)

#### pub fn [closure_ref](https://docs.rs#method.closure_ref)<'a, C>(closure: &'a [ScopedClosure](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/closure/struct.ScopedClosure.html)<'_, C>) -> &'a Self

Convert a borrowed `ScopedClosure` into a typed JavaScript Function reference.

The conversion is a direct type-safe conversion and upcast of a
closure into its corresponding typed JavaScript Function,
based on covariance and contravariance [ Upcast](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/convert/traits/trait.Upcast.html) trait hierarchy.

For transferring ownership to JS, use [ Function::from_closure](https://docs.rs/struct.Function.html#method.from_closure).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#4919-4926)#### pub fn [from_closure](https://docs.rs#method.from_closure)<C>(closure: [ScopedClosure](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/closure/struct.ScopedClosure.html)<'static, C>) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#4919-4926)

#### pub fn [from_closure](https://docs.rs#method.from_closure)<C>(closure: [ScopedClosure](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/closure/struct.ScopedClosure.html)<'static, C>) -> Self

Convert a Rust closure into a typed JavaScript Function.

This function releases ownership of the closure to JS, and provides an owned function handle for the same closure.

The conversion is a direct type-safe conversion and upcast of a
closure into its corresponding typed JavaScript Function,
based on covariance and contravariance [ Upcast](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/convert/traits/trait.Upcast.html) trait hierarchy.

This method is only supported for static closures which do not have borrowed lifetime data, and thus can be released into JS.

For borrowed closures, which cannot cede ownership to JS,
instead use [ Function::closure_ref](https://docs.rs/struct.Function.html#method.closure_ref).

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

The `forEach()` method executes a provided function once per array
element. This method has the same algorithm as
`Array.prototype.forEach()`. `TypedArray` is one of the typed array
types here.

Creates a JS typed array which is a view into wasm’s linear memory at the slice specified.

This function returns a new typed array which is a view into wasm’s memory. This view does not copy the underlying data.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Views into WebAssembly memory are only valid so long as the
backing buffer isn’t resized in JS. Once this function is called
any future calls to `Box::new` (or malloc of any form) may cause
the returned value here to be invalidated. Use with caution!

Additionally the returned object can be safely mutated but the input slice isn’t guaranteed to be mutable.

Finally, the returned object is disconnected from the input slice’s lifetime, so there’s no guarantee that the data is read at the right time.

Creates a JS typed array which is a view into wasm’s linear memory at the specified pointer with specified length.

This function returns a new typed array which is a view into wasm’s memory. This view does not copy the underlying data.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

Views into WebAssembly memory are only valid so long as the
backing buffer isn’t resized in JS. Once this function is called
any future calls to `Box::new` (or malloc of any form) may cause
the returned value here to be invalidated. Use with caution!

Additionally the returned object can be safely mutated, the changes are guaranteed to be reflected in the input array.

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

Creates a JS typed array which is a view into wasm’s linear memory at the slice specified.

This function returns a new typed array which is a view into wasm’s memory. This view does not copy the underlying data.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Views into WebAssembly memory are only valid so long as the
backing buffer isn’t resized in JS. Once this function is called
any future calls to `Box::new` (or malloc of any form) may cause
the returned value here to be invalidated. Use with caution!

Additionally the returned object can be safely mutated but the input slice isn’t guaranteed to be mutable.

Finally, the returned object is disconnected from the input slice’s lifetime, so there’s no guarantee that the data is read at the right time.

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

Creates a JS typed array which is a view into wasm’s linear memory at the slice specified.

This function returns a new typed array which is a view into wasm’s memory. This view does not copy the underlying data.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Views into WebAssembly memory are only valid so long as the
backing buffer isn’t resized in JS. Once this function is called
any future calls to `Box::new` (or malloc of any form) may cause
the returned value here to be invalidated. Use with caution!

Additionally the returned object can be safely mutated but the input slice isn’t guaranteed to be mutable.

Finally, the returned object is disconnected from the input slice’s lifetime, so there’s no guarantee that the data is read at the right time.

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

#### pub fn [next](https://docs.rs#method.next)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[IteratorNext](https://docs.rs/struct.IteratorNext.html)<T>, [JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html)>

The `next()` method always has to return an object with appropriate
properties including done and value. If a non-object value gets returned
(such as false or undefined), a TypeError (“iterator.next() returned a
non-object value”) will be thrown.

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#188)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#191)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#194)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

# JsOption in js_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/js-sys/0.3.103/js_sys/struct.JsOption.html

`pub struct JsOption<T = `[JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html)> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

An optional JS value of type `T`.

Unlike `Option<T>`, which is a Rust-side construct, `JsOption<T>` represents
a JS value that may be `T` or `undefined`, where the presence status is
not yet known in Rust. The value remains in JS until inspected via methods
like [ is_empty](https://docs.rs/struct.JsOption.html#method.is_empty),

[, or](https://docs.rs/struct.JsOption.html#method.as_option)

`as_option`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.JsOption.html#method.into_option)

`into_option`Only `undefined` is treated as absent, matching TypeScript’s `T | undefined`.
JavaScript `null` is a distinct present value.

`T` must implement [ JsGeneric](https://docs.rs/trait.JsGeneric.html), meaning it is any type that can be
represented as a

`JsValue` (e.g., `JsString`, `Number`, `Object`, etc.).
`JsOption<T>` itself implements `JsGeneric`, so it can be used in all
generic positions that accept JS types.## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Returns `JsOption::wrap(val)` if `Some(val)`, otherwise `JsOption::new()`.

Converts this `JsOption<T>` to an `Option<T>` by cloning the inner value.

Returns `None` if the value is `undefined`, otherwise returns

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#9151)

#### pub fn [char_code_at](https://docs.rs#method.char_code_at)(&self, index: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)

The `charCodeAt()` method returns an integer between 0 and 65535
representing the UTF-16 code unit at the given index (the UTF-16 code
unit matches the Unicode code point for code points representable in a
single UTF-16 code unit, but might also be the first code unit of a
surrogate pair for code points not representable in a single UTF-16 code
unit, e.g. Unicode code points > 0x10000).  If you want the entire code
point value, use `codePointAt()`.

Returns `NaN` if index is out of range.

the specified sequence of UTF-16 code units.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#9850-9852)#### pub fn [is_valid_utf16](https://docs.rs#method.is_valid_utf16)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#9850-9852)

#### pub fn [is_valid_utf16](https://docs.rs#method.is_valid_utf16)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Returns whether this string is a valid UTF-16 string.

This is useful for learning whether `String::from(..)` will return a
lossless representation of the JS string. If this string contains
unpaired surrogates then `String::from` will succeed but it will be a
lossy representation of the JS string because unpaired surrogates will
become replacement characters.

If this function returns `false` then to get a lossless representation
of the string you’ll need to manually use the `iter` method (or the
`char_code_at` accessor) to view the raw character codes.

For more information, see the documentation on [JS strings vs Rust
strings](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html)

Returns an iterator over the `u16` character codes that make up this JS
string.

This method will call `char_code_at` for each code in this JS string,
returning an iterator of the codes in sequence.

If this string consists of a single Unicode code point, then this method
converts it into a Rust `char` without doing any allocations.

If this JS value is not a valid UTF-8 or consists of more than a single
codepoint, then this returns `None`.

Note that a single Unicode code point might be represented as more than
one code unit on the JavaScript side. For example, a JavaScript string
`"\uD801\uDC37"` is actually a single Unicode code point U+10437 which
corresponds to a character ‘𐐷’.

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

# Null in js_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/js-sys/0.3.103/js_sys/struct.Null.html

`pub struct Null { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The JavaScript `null` value.

This type represents the JavaScript `null` primitive value and can be
used as a generic type parameter to indicate that a value is `null`.

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#191)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#194)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

# SharedArrayBuffer in js_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/js-sys/0.3.103/js_sys/struct.SharedArrayBuffer.html

The SharedArrayBuffer object is used to represent a generic,
fixed-length raw binary data buffer, similar to the ArrayBuffer
object, but in a way that they can be used to create views
on shared memory. Unlike an ArrayBuffer, a SharedArrayBuffer
cannot become detached.

The SharedArrayBuffer object is used to represent a generic,
fixed-length raw binary data buffer, similar to the ArrayBuffer
object, but in a way that they can be used to create views
on shared memory. Unlike an ArrayBuffer, a SharedArrayBuffer
cannot become detached.

The byteLength accessor property represents the length of
an SharedArrayBuffer in bytes. This is established when
the SharedArrayBuffer is constructed and cannot be changed.

The maxByteLength accessor property of SharedArrayBuffer instances returns the maximum
length (in bytes) that this SharedArrayBuffer can be resized to.

The slice() method returns a new SharedArrayBuffer whose contents
are a copy of this SharedArrayBuffer’s bytes from begin, inclusive,
up to end, exclusive.

The slice() method returns a new SharedArrayBuffer whose contents
are a copy of this SharedArrayBuffer’s bytes from begin, inclusive,
up to end, exclusive.

The hasOwnProperty() method returns a boolean indicating whether the
object has the specified property as its own property (as opposed to
inheriting it).

The toLocaleString() method returns a string representing the object.
This method is meant to be overridden by derived objects for
locale-specific purposes.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust String.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
JsString::try_from() function from js-sys
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns None.

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
documentation about the str type which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

The type that holds the reference to Self for the duration of the
invocation of the function that has an &Self parameter. This is
required to ensure that the lifetimes don’t persist beyond one function
call, and so that they remain anonymous.

Construct the wire representation for Some(slice). The returned
WasmSlice is either a borrow of the input slice (primitive
case) or a buffer JS owns and frees (handle-shaped case).

Wire representation for None (used by Option<&[T]>). A null
WasmSlice (ptr == 0) is the convention shared with every
other vector-like ABI in the crate.

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings

different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns

Creates a JS typed array which is a view into wasm’s linear memory at the slice specified.

This function returns a new typed array which is a view into wasm’s memory. This view does not copy the underlying data.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Views into WebAssembly memory are only valid so long as the
backing buffer isn’t resized in JS. Once this function is called
any future calls to `Box::new` (or malloc of any form) may cause
the returned value here to be invalidated. Use with caution!

Additionally the returned object can be safely mutated but the input slice isn’t guaranteed to be mutable.

Finally, the returned object is disconnected from the input slice’s lifetime, so there’s no guarantee that the data is read at the right time.

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

Creates a JS typed array which is a view into wasm’s linear memory at the slice specified.

This function returns a new typed array which is a view into wasm’s memory. This view does not copy the underlying data.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Views into WebAssembly memory are only valid so long as the
backing buffer isn’t resized in JS. Once this function is called
any future calls to `Box::new` (or malloc of any form) may cause
the returned value here to be invalidated. Use with caution!

Additionally the returned object can be safely mutated but the input slice isn’t guaranteed to be mutable.

Finally, the returned object is disconnected from the input slice’s lifetime, so there’s no guarantee that the data is read at the right time.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#14136-14180)#### pub unsafe fn [view_mut_raw](https://docs.rs#method.view_mut_raw)(ptr: [*mut ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html)[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html), length: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [Uint32Array](https://docs.rs/struct.Uint32Array.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

Views into WebAssembly memory are only valid so long as the

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#188)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#191)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#194)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

# Undefined in js_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/js-sys/0.3.103/js_sys/struct.Undefined.html

`pub struct Undefined { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The JavaScript `undefined` value.

This type represents the JavaScript `undefined` primitive value and can be
used as a generic type parameter to indicate that a value is `undefined`.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#188)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#191)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#194)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

# WeakMap in js_sys - Rust

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

The [ WeakMap](https://docs.rs/struct.WeakMap.html) object is a collection of key/value pairs in which the
keys are weakly referenced.  The keys must be objects and the values can
be arbitrary values.

# IntoJsGeneric in js_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/js-sys/0.3.103/js_sys/trait.IntoJsGeneric.html

```
pub trait IntoJsGeneric {
    type
```
[JsCanon](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.JsCanon): [JsGeneric](https://docs.rs/trait.JsGeneric.html);
    // Required method
    fn [to_js](https://docs.rs#tymethod.to_js)(self) -> Self::[JsCanon](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoJsGeneric.html#associatedtype.JsCanon);
}## Expand description

Value conversion from a type into its canonical [ JsGeneric](https://docs.rs/trait.JsGeneric.html) form.

This trait allows types to be converted into JsGeneric supported types, which are required to be erasably generic with JsValue.

The single associated type — rather than a free type parameter bounded by
`AsRef<T>` — is what makes collection-style APIs infer annotation-free.
Given an input `A`, there is exactly one `A::JsCanon`, so rustc never has
to search across multiple `AsRef` impls to pick a target element type.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementations-1)Implementations

Provided impls:

- `JsValue`
- Every `#[wasm_bindgen]`-imported type (identity — emitted by the macro).
- Every generic `js_sys`container (`Array<T>`,`Promise<T>`,`Set<T>`, …) provides its own identity impl owned by`js_sys`.
- References to cloneable implementors, so borrowed iteration can still produce owned JS-generic values.

This trait is deliberately *not* blanket-implemented over all [ JsGeneric](https://docs.rs/trait.JsGeneric.html)
types: each implementor explicitly opts in, which leaves room for future
wrapper types to pick a non-identity

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoJsGeneric.html#associatedtype.JsCanon)

`Self::JsCanon`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

# JsGeneric in js_sys - Rust

```
pub trait JsGeneric:

```
[ErasableGeneric](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/__rt/marker/trait.ErasableGeneric.html)<Repr = [JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html)>
    + [UpcastFrom](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/convert/traits/trait.UpcastFrom.html)<Self>
    + [Upcast](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/convert/traits/trait.Upcast.html)<Self>
    + [Upcast](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/convert/traits/trait.Upcast.html)<[JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html)>

A convenience trait for types that erase to [ JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html).

This is a shorthand for `ErasableGeneric<Repr = JsValue>`, used as a bound
on generic parameters that must be representable as JavaScript values.

[§](https://docs.rs#when-to-use)When to Use

Use `JsGeneric` as a trait bound when you need a generic type that:

- Can be passed to/from JavaScript
- Is type-erased to `JsValue`at the FFI boundary

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use wasm_bindgen::JsGeneric;
fn process_js_values<T: JsGeneric>(items: &[T]) {
    // T can be any JS-compatible type
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementors-1)Implementors

This trait is automatically implemented for all types that implement
`ErasableGeneric<Repr = JsValue>`, including:

- All `js_sys`types (`Object`,`Array`,`Function`, etc.)
- `JsValue`itself
- Custom types imported via `#[wasm_bindgen]`

# Iterable in js_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/js-sys/0.3.103/js_sys/trait.Iterable.html

```
pub trait Iterable {
    type
```
[Item](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Item);
}## Expand description

Trait for JavaScript types that implement the iterable protocol via `Symbol.iterator`.

Types implementing this trait can be iterated over using JavaScript’s iteration
protocol. The `Item` associated type specifies the type of values yielded.

[§](https://docs.rs#built-in-iterables)Built-in Iterables

Many `js-sys` collection types implement `Iterable` out of the box:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use js_sys::{Array, Map, Set};
// Array<T> yields T
let arr: Array<Number> = get_numbers();
for value in arr.iter() {
    let num: Number = value?;
}
// Map<K, V> yields Array (key-value pairs)
let map: Map<JsString, Number> = get_map();
for entry in map.iter() {
    let pair: Array = entry?;
}
// Set<T> yields T
let set: Set<JsString> = get_set();
for value in set.iter() {
    let s: JsString = value?;
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#typing-foreign-iterators)Typing Foreign Iterators

If you have a JavaScript value that implements the iterator protocol (has a `next()`
method) but isn’t a built-in type, you can use [ JsCast](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/cast/trait.JsCast.html) to cast it to

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Iterator.html)

`Iterator<T>`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use js_sys::Iterator;
use wasm_bindgen::JsCast;
// For a value you know implements the iterator protocol
fn process_iterator(js_iter: JsValue) {
    // Checked cast - returns None if not an iterator
    if let Some(iter) = js_iter.dyn_ref::<Iterator<Number>>() {
        for value in iter.into_iter() {
            let num: Number = value.unwrap();
            // ...
        }
    }
}
// Or with unchecked cast when you're certain of the type
fn process_known_iterator(js_iter: JsValue) {
    let iter: &Iterator<JsString> = js_iter.unchecked_ref();
    for value in iter.into_iter() {
        let s: JsString = value.unwrap();
        // ...
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-with-jsvalue)Using with `JsValue`

For dynamic or unknown iterables, use [ try_iter](https://docs.rs/fn.try_iter.html) which returns an untyped iterator:

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

# Promising in js_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/js-sys/0.3.103/js_sys/trait.Promising.html

```
pub trait Promising {
    type
```
[Resolution](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Resolution);
}## Expand description

Marker trait for types which represent `Resolution` or `Promise<Resolution>`.

For all types except for `Promise`, `Resolution` is equal to the type itself.
For `Promise` or any thenable or type extending Promise, `Resolution` is the
type of the promise resolution.

Manually implementing this trait is only required for custom thenables or
types which extend Promise. To disable automatic implementation, use the
`#[wasm_bindgen(no_promising)]` attribute.

The `encodeURI()` function encodes a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI)

# js_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/js-sys/latest/js_sys/

## Expand description

Bindings to JavaScript’s standard, built-in objects, including their methods and properties.

This does *not* include any Web, Node, or any other JS environment
APIs. Only the things that are guaranteed to exist in the global scope by
the ECMAScript standard.

[§](https://docs.rs#a-note-about-camelcase-snake_case-and-naming-conventions)A Note About `camelCase`, `snake_case`, and Naming Conventions

JavaScript’s global objects use `camelCase` naming conventions for functions
and methods, but Rust style is to use `snake_case`. These bindings expose
the Rust style `snake_case` name. Additionally, acronyms within a method
name are all lower case, where as in JavaScript they are all upper case. For
example, `decodeURI` in JavaScript is exposed as `decode_uri` in these
bindings.

[§](https://docs.rs#a-note-about-tostring-and-to_js_string)A Note About `toString` and `to_js_string`

JavaScript’s `toString()` method is exposed as `to_js_string()` in these
bindings to avoid confusion with Rust’s [ ToString](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/trait.ToString.html) trait and its

`to_string()` method. This allows types to implement both the Rust
[trait (which provides](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html)

`Display``to_string()` via
[) and still expose the JavaScript](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/trait.ToString.html)

`ToString``toString()` functionality.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [wasm_bindgen](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/index.html);

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

# cfg-if

A macro to ergonomically define an item depending on a large number of #[cfg] parameters. Structured like an if-else chain, the first matching branch is the item that gets emitted.

# wasm-bindgen 0.2.126 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wasm-bindgen/=0.2.126

Built with 🦀🕸 by The Rust and WebAssembly Working Group

## Install `wasm-bindgen-cli`

You can install it using `cargo install`:

```
cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli
```
Or, you can download it from the
[release page](https://github.com/wasm-bindgen/wasm-bindgen/releases).

If you have [ cargo-binstall](https://crates.io/crates/cargo-binstall) installed,
then you can install the pre-built artifacts by running:

```
cargo binstall wasm-bindgen-cli
```
## Example

Import JavaScript things into Rust and export Rust things to JavaScript.

```
use *;
// Import the `window.alert` function from the Web.
extern "C"
// Export a `greet` function from Rust to JavaScript, that alerts a
// hello message.
```
Use exported Rust things from JavaScript with ECMAScript modules!

```
import  from "./hello_world";
;
```
## Features

-
**Lightweight.**Only pay for what you use.`wasm-bindgen`only generates bindings and glue for the JavaScript imports you actually use and Rust functionality that you export. For example, importing and using the`document.querySelector`method doesn't cause`Node.prototype.appendChild`or`window.alert`to be included in the bindings as well.
-
**ECMAScript modules.**Just import WebAssembly modules the same way you would import JavaScript modules. Future compatible with[WebAssembly modules and ECMAScript modules integration](https://github.com/WebAssembly/esm-integration).
-
**Designed with the**Eventually, there won't be any JavaScript shims between Rust-generated wasm functions and native DOM methods. Because the Wasm functions are statically type checked, some of those native methods' dynamic type checks should become unnecessary, promising to unlock even-faster-than-JavaScript DOM access.["Web IDL bindings" proposal](https://github.com/WebAssembly/proposals/issues/8)in mind.

## Guide

## API Docs

## MSRV Policy

- Libraries that are released on [crates.io](https://crates.io)have a MSRV of v1.77.
- CLI tools and their corresponding support libraries have a MSRV of v1.86.

The project aims to maintain a 2-year MSRV policy for libraries (meaning we support Rust versions released within the last 2 years), but with a shorter MSRV policy for the CLI. Changes to the MSRV may be made in patch versions, and will be logged in the CHANGELOG and MSRV history below.

### MSRV History

| Version | Library MSRV | CLI MSRV | Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.2.118 | 1.77 | 1.86 | 2026-04-10 |
| 0.2.106 | 1.71 | 1.82 | 2025-11-27 |
| 0.2.103 | 1.57 | 1.82 | 2025-09-17 |
| 0.2.93 | 1.57 | 1.76 | 2024-08-13 |

# futures-lite 2.6.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/futures-lite/^2

# futures-lite

A lightweight async prelude.

This crate is a subset of [futures](https://docs.rs/futures) that compiles an order of magnitude faster, fixes minor
warts in its API, fills in some obvious gaps, and removes almost all unsafe code from it.

In short, this crate aims to be more enjoyable than [futures](https://docs.rs/futures) but still fully compatible with
it.

The API for this crate is intentionally constrained. Please consult the
[features list](https://github.com/smol-rs/futures-lite/blob/master/FEATURES.md) for APIs that are occluded from this crate.

## Examples

```
use future;
```
